legend: Pagetoid proliferation of large atypical epithelioid cells in the epidermis.

Schematic figure illustrating the classification of lymphocytic infiltrate patterns in vertical growth phase (VGP) melanomas, as defined by Clark and colleagues. A A lymphocytic infiltrate pattern is classified as “brisk” when TILs diffusely infiltrate the entire invasive component of the tumour (“diffuse”, left panel) or when they infiltrate the entire base of the tumour (“peripheral”, right panel). B Isolated, multifocal, and segmental TIL infiltrate patterns are classified as “non-brisk”. C A VGP melanoma is classified as having an “absent” TIL pattern when no TILs are infiltrating tumour tissue (top-left panel) or when lymphocytes are confined to perivascular areas (top-right panel) or to areas of fibrosis (bottom-left panel). In cases where there are multiple tumour nodules, the overall TIL grade should be determined by the grade of the nodule with the lowest number of TILs (bottom-right panel).

legend: The papillary dermis is widened with fibroplasia, and there is a sprinkling of lymphocytes and melanophages, consistent with a regressed pigmented lesion.

Radial growth phase. There are atypical melanocytes with pagetoid scatter in the epidermis, as well as clusters of cells in the dermis resembling those in the epidermis and lacking evidence of tumorigenic proliferation or mitotic activity.

Radial growth phase (left) and vertical growth phase (right). The vertical growth phase is composed of uniformly atypical cells that fill and expand the papillary dermis and infiltrate the reticular dermis. Unlike the cells of a naevus, these cells do not mature and do not disperse into the reticular dermis.
This tumour has a radial growth phase component (plaque-like, predominantly tan, at the upper right of the lesion) and a vertical growth phase (raised, predominantly black).
